match.reason: The bank point covers stone tools and how they were made and used, but nothing on trade networks or goods like ochre and shells moving over long distances, which is the central idea of the new point.

rejected.title: Trade networks and technologies
card: Aboriginal Peoples traded goods across long distances. Ochre, stone axes and shells were passed from group to group along trade routes, often across many different Countries.
Goods could travel hundreds of kilometres, even though each group passed them on only part of the way. Where a stone or shell is found far from its source, it shows that trade took place.
Trade was more than swapping goods. It linked people, and it was often carried out through relationships and ceremony, so it also shared stories, songs and news.

Tools changed over time. A ground-edge axe has a stone head with its edge ground to a sharp, smooth finish. The oldest known ones from northern Australia are about 30,000 years old, among the oldest in the world.
rejected.remember: Trade moved goods and ideas across Country, and tools like ground-edge axes show technology changing over time.

a.q: Archaeologists find a shell ornament far inland, hundreds of kilometres from the sea. What does this most likely show?
opts: Goods were traded between groups over long distances
The group who found it had lived at the coast
Shells were only ever used for food and never traded
Each group made all its goods using local materials
a.why: A sea shell found far inland shows it was passed from group to group along trade routes. The idea that each group used only local materials is wrong, because the shell came from far away.
a.clue: How could a sea shell end up far from the sea?

b.q: A museum displays a ground-edge axe head and a much older flaked stone tool from the same region. What can historians learn by comparing them?
opts: Toolmaking changed over time as new techniques developed
Aboriginal Peoples had no technology before ground-edge axes
Ground-edge axes were never traded across long distances
The older tool was made by a different group of people
b.why: The two tools were made in different periods, using different methods, so they show technology changing over time. It does not follow that earlier people had no technology, because flaked stone tools were also skilled work.
b.clue: Think about what a change in tools shows about the past.

version.title: Trade networks and technologies
card: Aboriginal groups traded goods over long distances. Ochre (coloured earth used for painting and ceremony), stone axe heads and shells passed from group to group along trade routes, across many Countries.
Axe heads made from stone quarried at Mount William, on Wurundjeri Country north of Melbourne, have been found hundreds of kilometres away. Goods found far from their source are evidence of trade.
A ground-edge axe has a stone head whose edge was ground smooth and sharp against a rougher stone. A ground edge is stronger than a simple flaked edge and can be sharpened again.
Pieces of ground-edge axes found in the Kimberley are more than 40,000 years old, among the oldest found anywhere. Comparing tools from different times shows how technology changed.
version.remember: Goods found far from their source show trade, and tools from different times show technology changing.

a.q: Archaeologists dig up red ochre at a site far from any place where ochre is found naturally. What does this most likely show?
opts: It reached the site through trade between groups
It was made at the site from crushed local plants
It formed in the ground at the site over time
It shows the group never traded with neighbours
a.why: Ochre is a coloured earth, and this site is far from any source of it, so it was most likely passed along a trade route. It cannot have formed at the site or come from plants, because ochre comes from the earth at its source.
a.clue: How could something end up far from where it comes from?

b.q: At one site, tools dated to 20,000 years ago are all flaked stone, while tools dated to 3,000 years ago include ground-edge axes. What does this show?
opts: Toolmaking at the site changed over time
Earlier toolmakers at the site had less skill
Ground-edge axes were invented first at this site
Flaked tools stopped being used at the site
b.why: A new kind of tool appearing at a later time shows technology changing. A different method is not proof of less skill, and ground-edge axes far older than these have been found in the Kimberley.
b.clue: Compare the tools from the two dates.

a.best: It reached the site through trade between groups

b.best: Toolmaking at the site changed over time

check.summary: No problems found. The point is about Aboriginal histories and cultures, so it is marked first-nations for the owner's review.
